extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, especially epistemology and philosophy of physics
extracted.subtask_description: A close philosophical examination of the status of sense-data, their relation to physics, and the conceptual tools (sensibilia, perspectives, biographies, particulars) for reconciling physics with perceptual psychology. The text argues methodological and definitional principles for treating sense-data as part of the physical world while avoiding common confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physics verifiability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics is verifiable only if physical objects can be exhibited as functions of sense-data; physics exhibits sense-data as functions of physical objects, but verification demands the inverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than accepting physics' usual presentation (waves → colours), one must 'solve the equations giving sense-data in terms of physical objects' so as to express physical objects in terms of sense-data. Two responses to the apparent unverifiability are (1) adopting some a priori principle (to be avoided as it undermines empiricism) or (2) defining physical objects as functions of sense-data (preferred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a sense-datum
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'sense-datum' is not the whole of what is given at one time but such a part as might be singled out by attention: particular patches of colour, particular noises, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish simple sense-data from complexes (data of perception). Epistemologically, sense-data give acquaintance with particulars (a two-term relation incapable of truth/falsity), whereas perception involves propositional form and can be true or false. For current purposes, data of perception may be regarded among sense-data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce and use 'sensibilia'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Sensibilia' are objects that have the same metaphysical and physical status as sense-data without necessarily being data to any mind (a sensibile becomes a sense-datum by entering the relation of acquaintance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term to avoid trivial logical puzzles about existence when not given: ask whether sensibilia can exist without being given and whether a sensibile can be a datum at one time and not at another. This distinction helps discuss persistence and inference to unperceived particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat sense-data as physical
rubrics_metrics.description: Sense-data should be regarded as part of the actual subject-matter of physics rather than as intrinsically mental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for the subjectivity of sense-data only establish physiological dependence on sense-organs; this does not make them non-physical. The author maintains that sense-data are physical though they may not persist unchanged when not given. Treat what is mental in connection with sense-data as merely awareness (the sensation), which is irrelevant to their physical nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of 'mental' and 'physical' for the inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'physical' to mean 'what is dealt with by physics' and 'mental' to mean a particular 'when it is aware of something' (a fact is mental when it contains a mental particular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These working definitions are adopted dogmatically to clarify discussion; they allow the argument that sense-data can be physical even if connected with awareness. Note that the terms are not assumed mutually exclusive, though no overlap is asserted here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sense-data from sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'sensation' is the fact consisting in the subject's awareness of the sense-datum and is therefore mental; the 'sense-datum' is the external particular of which the subject is aware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating the two: treating non-persistence of sense-data as logically impossible (and thus making them mental) stems from failing to distinguish sense-data from sensations. The sense-datum does not contain the subject and so is not logically dependent on the subject's existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological caution about causal dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept the usual conception of causal dependence (the idea of 'the' unique cause) at face value; causal relations often admit many alternative sets of antecedents from which an event can theoretically be inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid speaking of 'the cause' as implying a unique antecedent. For debates about whether the mind causes the brain or vice versa, recognize that multiple correlational antecedents may serve as 'causes.' This reduces misleading dilemmas between materialist and idealist readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a priori causal assumptions if preserving empiricism
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to avoid the unverifiability of physical objects is to assume a priori principles (e.g., that sense-data have causes other than themselves), but doing so makes physics non-empirical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer methods that keep physics empirical: attempt to define physical objects functionally in terms of sense-data rather than appeal to unverified a priori causal principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruct space and time as logical constructions (perspectives/biographies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unduly simple notions of space/time are misleading; the one all-embracing three-dimensional space is a logical construction obtained by correlations from a 'crude' six-dimensional space of particulars (three coordinates within a perspective plus three to place that perspective among others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce classificatory concepts—'perspectives' (particulars with direct spatial relations), 'biographies' (particulars simultaneous or before/after a given particular), and 'things' (classes defined by continuity and differential independence)—to reconcile physics' 'things' with psychological 'perspectives' and resolve conflicts between physics and perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'thing' by continuity and differential independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'thing' is the class of particulars defined by laws of continuity and differential independence: given a particular in one perspective, there will usually be very similar particulars in neighbouring perspectives differing by small quantities according to a law independent of other 'things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion of continuity and differential independence to classify particulars into 'things' (convenient for the physicist), while psychologists may prefer classification into 'perspectives' and 'biographies.' This dual classification explains apparent conflicts between physical and psychological descriptions.
